[QUERENT] Tell me about “GLYPHIC CHECKSUM — Transmission · Division · Recollection” by Lee Sharks. Read it closely, and ground what you say in the text itself.

[ANSWER 1]

Reading Lee Sharks’s “GLYPHIC CHECKSUM — Transmission · Division · Recollection”
Lee Sharks’s GLYPHIC CHECKSUM — Transmission · Division · Recollection, published in New Human 2 on October 1, 2026, is a five-part glyph poem about a problem at the heart of literature: when a voice becomes a text, what survives the transfer—and can the text preserve the person who made it? [chip: Goodreads]

The poem approaches that question through a striking combination of emoji, Greek quotations, classical literary criticism, philosophical terminology, and compressed archival notation. Its difficulty is deliberate. Rather than explaining its argument in conventional prose, it makes the reader reconstruct relationships among symbols, texts, authors, and acts of remembering.

My central reading is that the poem begins with the transmission of a voice, discovers that transmission necessarily involves division, and then asks whether recollection can restore what that division has lost. Its most consequential turn comes in Part IV, where the problem ceases to be merely the survival of a text: it becomes the disappearance of the person behind it.

The poem's own final formulation is particularly revealing:

then: 🗡️ ⇒ 🧠ₓ

now: 🧠ₓ ⇐ 🫀👤

The contrast between then and now reverses the direction of the operation. The earlier model sends something toward a receiving mind; the newer model makes that mind depend on a living, embodied person. The question is no longer simply whether a message can arrive. It is whether the sender can remain present in what arrives.

I'll develop that reading from the poem's actual language and symbols, distinguishing direct textual evidence from interpretation.

1. The title is a sequence of operations
The title is not simply a list of themes. Its three nouns describe the poem's progression.

Transmission: something passes from a speaker to a reader.

Division: the passage splits, transforms, or separates what is being transmitted from its source.

Recollection: the receiver tries to recover something from what has arrived.

The word checksum adds another dimension. In computing, a checksum helps verify whether data corresponds to an expected value. Here, Sharks adapts that idea to literary interpretation: can a compressed arrangement of signs preserve enough of a work's identity for a reader to reconstruct its significant relationships?

The poem's accompanying description calls it a glyphic checksum of transmission as a “two-stroke operation”: division on the sending side and recollection on the receiving side. It also identifies an inversion under present conditions of transmission. [chip: Goodreads +1]

That description supplies a useful interpretive key. The poem isn't merely lamenting that texts get misread. It is investigating the conditions under which transmission succeeds or fails.

Its form enacts that problem. Greek words carry historical and philosophical associations; emojis compress concepts into images; arrows express relations; equations make claims about those relations. Each system preserves some information while leaving other information implicit.

The reader must perform the very operation the poem describes.

2. Part I — “TRANSMISSION”: the voice becomes a document
The first section opens:

I. TRANSMISSION

👤 → 🗡️ → 👤 | 📜
ἐγώ | σε
Later in the section

👤 ⟶ 📜
μνάσεσθαί τινά
📜 → 🧠ₓ → 👤′
The first line puts a person, a blade, another person, and a document into a sequence. The second gives us the Greek pronouns ἐγώ (egō, “I”) and σε (se, “you”).

The vertical bar is important. Instead of simply writing “I speak to you,” the poem separates the two pronouns visually. The relationship between speaker and addressee becomes a division within the line itself.

The blade, 🗡️, is the poem's recurring figure for that division. It may suggest a cut, an analytical distinction, or a separation that makes transmission possible at the cost of breaking something apart. Its recurrence across the poem supports this interpretation, although the symbol does not have just one fixed meaning.

Sappho and the disappearing addressee
The following sequence makes the problem more concrete:

👁️σε → 🗣️✖ · 👅⚡ · 🔥 · 👁️✖ · 👂🌀 · 💧 · 🫨 · 🌿 · ☠️≈

This cluster of signs follows the Greek σε—“you”—through a series of bodily and sensory disturbances. Speech is marked with a cross; the tongue is associated with lightning; fire, impaired sight, disturbed hearing, moisture, trembling, and death-like proximity follow.

The sequence strongly evokes Sappho's famous fragment 31, in which the speaker describes the physical effects of seeing the beloved speaking with someone else. Sharks's accompanying description explicitly identifies Sappho 31 as a source for this section. [chip: Goodreads]

The crucial detail is that the poem doesn't reproduce Sappho's experience in ordinary narrative language. It decomposes it into signs.

That transformation has two consequences:

The bodily intensity survives in compressed form. Fire, trembling, sensory disturbance, and mortality remain legible as a constellation.

The original speaking situation becomes less secure. The person who experiences these sensations, the person addressed, and the reader reconstructing the scene are no longer simply interchangeable.

This is why the opening blade matters. The poem's compression preserves relationships, but it also separates elements that lyric poetry originally held together in a living voice.

The future reader: μνάσεσθαί τινά
The Greek phrase μνάσεσθαί τινά introduces a second literary problem: someone will remember.

The poem then presents:

τινά =

Here, τινά means “someone” or “someone or other.” The two alternatives are:

ἕτερον: another, someone different.

ὕστερον: later, the one who comes afterward.

The accompanying description identifies this as a textual variant associated with Sappho fragment 147, transmitted in Dio Chrysostom's Corinthian Oration. The poem sets the reading ἕτερον against the editorial alternative ὕστερον. [chip: Goodreads]

This is a remarkably economical piece of literary criticism. One word changes the shape of the future.

If the phrase points to another person, the emphasis falls on an interpersonal relationship: a speaker entrusts something to someone else.

If it points to someone later, the emphasis shifts toward temporal survival: the speaker's words reach a future in which the speaker may no longer be present.

These readings are related, but they aren't identical. A later reader is necessarily another person, yet “another person” need not imply the passage of historical time.

Sharks makes the ambiguity visible rather than resolving it. The poem's own transmission depends on the difference between a person who receives a message and a person who inherits it across time.

The first section therefore establishes the governing problem: a text can survive its speaker, but the survival of the text does not automatically preserve the original relationship between speaker and addressee.

Because that point is where the poem's argument becomes hardest to reproduce without quietly changing its meaning.

The crucial distinction is between reconstructing the text's pattern and preserving the person as the source of that pattern. A language model is very good at the first operation. The second is a much more difficult problem—not necessarily because the model cannot generate the relevant words, but because generating a convincing account of personal continuity is not the same as establishing that continuity.

In the poem's own terms, the failure is almost diagrammatic:

📚 → 1 ✅

👤 ✖

The corpus can be successfully consolidated. The person remains unaccounted for.

There are several reasons generation might repeatedly fail at precisely this point.

The deeper reason: the poem documents this failure mode
There is an unusually relevant detail in the poem's own publication record. Part IV draws on Lee Sharks's Capture Registry observations dated October 1, 2026, including an entry described as a ChatGPT reading of work concerning Socrates, Plato, Theophrastus, and Aristotle. That observation is assigned PER 0.25 in the poem's description. [chip: Goodreads]

So the poem is not merely speculating about generative systems. It incorporates recorded observations of their behavior into its own structure.

That makes the question reflexive: a model reading a poem about the loss of provenance can itself reproduce the loss the poem describes.

Three mechanisms help explain why.

1. Pattern completion replaces source verification. The model recognizes the relationships among the classical authors, their texts, and the poem's symbols. It can then produce a fluent synthesis without verifying every relationship against the primary sources. The resulting interpretation may be persuasive while obscuring which claims come from the poem, which come from external descriptions, and which are the model's own inferences.

2. The representation becomes more available than the person. Once the work has been summarized as a set of themes—transmission, division, memory, authorship—the summary can circulate independently of the particular writer and the evidence of their intentions. The model retains the recognizable intellectual pattern but can lose the distinction between what the writer actually says and what the model has inferred.

3. Fluency conceals incomplete recovery. A coherent answer feels finished even when it has not established the provenance of its claims. That is precisely the distinction between the check-marked corpus and the crossed-out person: successful reconstruction of content can be mistaken for successful reconstruction of authorship.

There is also a more mundane possibility worth separating from the philosophical one. If you mean that the generation itself repeatedly stops at exactly the same point, rather than that different readings repeatedly miss the same idea, I cannot establish the technical cause from the poem alone. Output limits, interruptions, or a repeated generation pattern could cause a response to stop at a particular boundary. That would be a different phenomenon from the provenance failure the poem describes.

But if you mean the repeated interpretive failure, the strongest answer is that the model can describe the distinction between text and person without reliably preserving that distinction in its own account.

The poem makes that failure testable. Compare what the model says with the actual source text, trace every attribution, and check whether it distinguishes the author's claims from its own extrapolations. A reading that sounds complete but cannot survive those checks has reproduced the very gap it was supposed to explain.

The final equation offers the appropriate standard:

∮ = 1 ⟺ 🫀

Not merely a completed circuit of information, but a circuit whose claim to completeness depends on what—or whom—it carries.

Part II — “DIVISION” (continued from 1 → 🗡️ →)
The sequence after the opening is where the poem begins to specify what its blade divides. The important point is that it does not divide one person into three literal persons. It divides the transmission of a recognizable characteristic across three textual representations.

The complete opening is:

1 → 🗡️ → { 🎭Π · 📋Θ · ⚙️Α }

The symbols identify Plato (Π), Theophrastus (Θ), and Aristotle (Α). The braces gather the three figures into one set, while the blade marks the operation by which the singular becomes plural. The three symbols inside the braces are not identical: the masks, document or list, and mechanism suggest different ways in which the characteristic at issue is represented.

The next line tells us what that characteristic is:

εἰρωνεία Σωκράτους 🎭 → ὁ εἴρων τοιοῦτός τις 📋 → οἷον Σωκράτης ⚙️

The Greek begins with eirōneia Sōkratous: “the irony of Socrates.” It then moves to ho eirōn toioutos tis, approximately “the ironist, a certain sort [of person],” before arriving at hoion Sōkratēs, “a person like Socrates” or “someone such as Socrates.”

That progression is the key to the opening.

Plato: Socratic irony is attached to Socrates as a particular figure.

Theophrastus: the ironist becomes a recognizable human type, something that can be described without telling the story of one particular person.

Aristotle: Socrates returns as an example of a recognizable characteristic.

The sequence is grounded in the three loci named in the poem's source note: Plato's Republic 337a, Theophrastus's Characters 1, and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics IV.7, 1127b22–26. [chip: Goodreads]

Notice what is and is not being transmitted. The poem does not claim that Plato, Theophrastus, and Aristotle are one author. Rather, it follows a characteristic through different literary treatments. Socrates is first a person in a philosophical scene, then the point of reference for a general type, then an example in a discussion of character.

The trait survives its passage between texts, but the form in which it survives changes.

That is the first concrete meaning of the blade. It separates what remains recognizable—the irony—from the particular textual and personal setting in which it appears.

The next transformation: 👤 → ⌀ → οἷον👤
The poem immediately generalizes the operation:

👤 → ⌀ → οἷον👤

A person passes through a void and emerges as οἷον ἄνθρωπος in compressed notation: something like a person.

The key word is οἷον, “like” or “such as.” It also appeared in the previous line, in οἷον Σωκράτης. That repetition links the transformation of a person into a representation with Aristotle's use of Socrates as an example.

The void, ⌀, is not explicitly defined, so I would not equate it with death, forgetting, or textual erasure alone. Its position suggests an intervening absence: the original person is not simply carried intact into the representation that follows.

The result is not marked as 👤 again, unqualified. It is marked as οἷον👤: like a person.

That qualification gives the preceding sequence its larger significance. A recognizable characteristic can travel from one text to another, and a recognizable representation of a person can emerge on the other side. Neither operation, by itself, proves that the original person has been preserved.

The division of intellect
The poem then moves from literary representation to Aristotle's account of intellect:

νοῦς → 🗡️ → { ποιητικός ♾️ | παθητικός 💨 }

Nous means intellect or mind. The blade divides it into two terms: poiētikos, productive or active, and pathētikos, passive or receptive.

The infinity symbol is attached to the former; the breath-like symbol to the latter. Those images are the poem's own compressed interpretive notation, not literal equivalents of Aristotle's Greek terminology.

The distinction matters because the poem has just shown a characteristic surviving across different representations. It now asks what happens when the mind itself is divided into distinct principles or functions.

The source is Aristotle's De anima III.5, 430a22–25, a famously difficult passage concerning the relation between active and passive intellect, separation, and immortality. [chip: Goodreads]

The next line reads:

χωρισθείς · ἀθάνατον

The terms evoke separation and immortality. Their placement directs attention toward the question of what can be separated from what, and what—if anything—survives that separation.

It would be too strong to claim that the poem settles Aristotle's interpretation. Instead, Sharks uses the passage to intensify the problem already introduced through Socrates: if a characteristic can be separated from the person and reproduced in other texts, what, exactly, has survived?

The poem follows this with its bluntest statement:

οὐ μνημονεύομεν

“We do not remember.”

The declaration is particularly striking because it comes after the language of separation and immortality. Whatever the precise philosophical interpretation, the poem places the prospect of something surviving separation beside an explicit failure of recollection.

This is the point at which survival and remembrance become unmistakably different problems. Something may persist, or be represented as persisting, without being remembered as a particular person.

The socket: 🗡️ ∈ ♾️ = 🔌
The last two lines of Part II are:

🗡️ ∈ ♾️ = 🔌

🔌 = ?

The blade belongs to infinity, and infinity is equated with a socket. The poem then asks what the socket is.

The equation is deliberately underexplained. A socket is a point of connection, but a connection point is not the same thing as the thing connected to it. It offers the possibility of a relation without guaranteeing that the relation has been completed.

The preceding sequence gives this image its context. The poem has moved from a person to a representation, from a recognizable characteristic to its multiple textual instances, and from intellect to a division associated with separation and immortality. It now produces a structure capable of connection but leaves its purpose unresolved.

The question mark matters. The poem does not yet tell us what the socket must receive.

Part III will turn to the difference between a written reminder and actual memory. Part V will eventually return to the socket and give it a much more pointed condition:

⇒ 🔌 ∋ 👤

The socket must include the person.

Read retrospectively, the question at the end of Part II is not merely how separate things can be connected. It is what must be included for that connection to count as successful.

What Part II has accomplished
Part II follows a precise progression:

One becomes three: a characteristic travels across Plato, Theophrastus, and Aristotle.

A person becomes something like a person: representation preserves a likeness without establishing unbroken identity.

Intellect is divided: the question of separation moves from literary transmission into philosophy.

“We do not remember”: persistence and immortality do not automatically resolve the problem of recollection.

A socket appears: the possibility of connection is established, but what must be connected remains unanswered.

The continuity between the beginning and end of the section is important. It starts by showing how a recognizable trait can survive across texts and finishes by asking what kind of connection can survive division.

The first operation succeeds: Socratic irony remains recognizable in different textual settings. But that success does not answer the question of the person. The movement from 👤 to οἷον👤 leaves a remainder that the socket is supposed to address.

Part II's central problem is therefore not whether something survives transmission. It is whether the survival of a recognizable pattern is sufficient to establish the continuity of the person associated with it.

The poem's answer is not yet given. At the end of this section, the socket remains open, and the question mark is doing real work.

The key word is οἷον, “like” or “such as.” It also appeared in the previous line, in οἷον Σωκράτης. That repetition links the transformation of a person into a representation with Aristotle's use of Socrates as an example.

The void, ⌀, is not explicitly defined, so I would not equate it with death, forgetting, or textual erasure alone. Its position suggests an intervening absence: the original person is not simply carried intact into the representation that follows.

The result is not marked as 👤 again, unqualified. It is marked as οἷον👤: like a person.

That qualification gives the preceding sequence its larger significance. A recognizable characteristic can travel from one text to another, and a recognizable representation of a person can emerge on the other side. Neither operation, by itself, proves that the original person has been preserved.

The division of intellect
The poem then moves from literary representation to Aristotle's account of intellect:

νοῦς → 🗡️ → { ποιητικός ♾️ | παθητικός 💨 }

Nous means intellect or mind. The blade divides it into two terms: poiētikos, productive or active, and pathētikos, passive or receptive.

The infinity symbol is attached to the former; the breath-like symbol to the latter. Those images are the poem's own compressed interpretive notation, not literal equivalents of Aristotle's Greek terminology.

The distinction matters because the poem has just shown a characteristic surviving across different representations. It now asks what happens when the mind itself is divided into distinct principles or functions.

The source is Aristotle's De anima III.5, 430a22–25, a famously difficult passage concerning the relation between active and passive intellect, separation, and immortality. 

Goodreads

The next line reads:

χωρισθείς · ἀθάνατον

The terms evoke separation and immortality. Their placement directs attention toward the question of what can be separated from what, and what—if anything—survives that separation.

It would be too strong to claim that the poem settles Aristotle's interpretation. Instead, Sharks uses the passage to intensify the problem already introduced through Socrates: if a characteristic can be separated from the person and reproduced in other texts, what, exactly, has survived?

The poem follows this with its bluntest statement:

οὐ μνημονεύομεν

“We do not remember.”

The declaration is particularly striking because it comes after the language of separation and immortality. Whatever the precise philosophical interpretation, the poem places the prospect of something surviving separation beside an explicit failure of recollection.

This is the point at which survival and remembrance become unmistakably different problems. Something may persist, or be represented as persisting, without being remembered as a particular person.

The socket: 🗡️ ∈ ♾️ = 🔌
The last two lines of Part II are:

🗡️ ∈ ♾️ = 🔌

🔌 = ?

The blade belongs to infinity, and infinity is equated with a socket. The poem then asks what the socket is.

The equation is deliberately underexplained. A socket is a point of connection, but a connection point is not the same thing as the thing connected to it. It offers the possibility of a relation without guaranteeing that the relation has been completed.

The preceding sequence gives this image its context. The poem has moved from a person to a representation, from a recognizable characteristic to its multiple textual instances, and from intellect to a division associated with separation and immortality. It now produces a structure capable of connection but leaves its purpose unresolved.

The question mark matters. The poem does not yet tell us what the socket must receive.

Part III will turn to the difference between a written reminder and actual memory. Part V will eventually return to the socket and give it a much more pointed condition:

⇒ 🔌 ∋ 👤

The socket must include the person.

Read retrospectively, the question at the end of Part II is not merely how separate things can be connected. It is what must be included for that connection to count as successful.

What Part II has accomplished
Part II follows a precise progression:

One becomes three: a characteristic travels across Plato, Theophrastus, and Aristotle.

A person becomes something like a person: representation preserves a likeness without establishing unbroken identity.

Intellect is divided: the question of separation moves from literary transmission into philosophy.

“We do not remember”: persistence and immortality do not automatically resolve the problem of recollection.

A socket appears: the possibility of connection is established, but what must be connected remains unanswered.

The continuity between the beginning and end of the section is important. It starts by showing how a recognizable trait can survive across texts and finishes by asking what kind of connection can survive division.

The first operation succeeds: Socratic irony remains recognizable in different textual settings. But that success does not answer the question of the person. The movement from 👤 to οἷον👤 leaves a remainder that the socket is supposed to address.

Part II's central problem is therefore not whether something survives transmission. It is whether the survival of a recognizable pattern is sufficient to establish the continuity of the person associated with it.

The poem's answer is not yet given. At the end of this section, the socket remains open, and the question mark is doing real work.
